transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-05 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Jon Ruiz (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Verdance CTO), Liam O'Neill (Verdance SRE), Dana Park (Product), Omar Rahman (Verdance Security)

Auto-summary: quick discovery; customer cares deeply about p95 for streaming tokens, needs predictable burst handling for campaign sends, and strong audit/KMS controls for EU customers.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, I'm an AE at Redwood. With me is Sofia, our SE, and Jon on the technical side. How are you all?
[00:10] Maya Singh: Hi Alex, thanks. Maya here, CTO at Verdance. We are, uh, excited to talk through latency and burst stuff.
[00:18] Liam O'Neill: Liam, SRE. We're preparing for a big summer marketing burst — some of our flows are real-time chat and others are streaming summarization.
[00:25] Alex Chen: Great. The goal for today is to understand your p95 targets, concurrency, streaming patterns, and what matters for hosting decisions — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:34] Dana Park: Quick callout, we have EU customers that require data residency and HSM-backed key management. So security's a gating item.
[00:44] Sofia Patel: Thanks Dana, we'll cover the security checklist. Maya, can you run us through current stack and numbers?
[00:52] Maya Singh: Sure. So currently we run an in-house inference farm on k8s, mixed GPU types, we get inconsistent latency. Typical daily steady-state is ~120 concurrent chat sessions, peak bursts up to 1,100 concurrent during promos. Average prompt length is 280 tokens, responses average 150 tokens. Our p95 target for streaming flows is 250ms end-to-end token latency — that's tough.
[01:20] Jon Ruiz: When you say 'end-to-end token latency' that's client to first token or per-token?
[01:25] Maya Singh: It's per-token streaming latency perceived by the user — so p95 of the server-side emission time plus network, we approximate server-side target at ~200ms p95.
[01:36] Sofia Patel: Understood. Are you using KV cache or prompt prefix caching today?
[01:40] Liam O'Neill: Not really, it's a blunt system — we do some application-level caching but not model KV.
[01:45] Alex Chen: Ok. In Redwood we have automatic prefix caching and KV cache options for repeated contexts — that usually helps with token/sec economics. Also batching config matters a lot for throughput/latency tradeoffs.
[01:57] Maya Singh: Can you talk about dedicated vs hosted? For steady-state we care about cost predictability; for bursts we care about headroom and SLOs.
[02:06] Alex Chen: Sure. Hosted gives you quickest path and dynamic scaling; Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and SLA-backed latency targets; Private gives you the VPC/air-gapped control. For a p95 of ~200ms server-side we generally recommend Dedicated with tuned kernels and prefix caching, unless you need strict on-prem residency.
[02:25] Dana Park: We probably want Dedicated for the primary workload, with an option to run Private in EU regions for regulated customers. Does Redwood support HSM KMS?
[02:34] Jon Ruiz: We integrate with customer KMS and HSM via our Private deployment. Hosted supports bring-your-own-key via cloud KMS in most regions — but for strict HSM you may need Private.
[02:43] Omar Rahman: And audit logs? We need immutable logs for each request and key rotation records.
[02:48] Sofia Patel: We provide request-level audit trails, token-level cost breakdowns, and retention policies. We'll include SOC2 docs and architecture diagrams.
[02:58] Liam O'Neill: On the performance side, how do you benchmark tokens/sec and p95 for streaming? We want to run our replay dataset against Redwood and compare to our baseline.
[03:07] Sofia Patel: Typical approach is: you give us representative traffic replay (anonymized), we run 48-hour profiling under two modes: Dedicated config (reserved capacity with KV cache) and Hosted scaled baseline. We collect p95 token latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and tail latency histograms. Then we surface recommended batch sizes, quantization level, and fallbacks.
[03:28] Maya Singh: What's the expected tokens/sec per GPU for our prompt/response profile?
[03:33] Jon Ruiz: Rough estimate depends on model variant; for an Llama-like 13B open model on A100-ish hardware with quantization we often see 4k–7k tokens/sec steady-state with batching; but streaming per-token latency is the constraint. If you want p95 server-side ~200ms we tune batching to very low latency (micro-batching) which reduces tokens/sec capacity per GPU — so you need more GPUs for the same throughput.
[03:56] Liam O'Neill: So it's a direct tradeoff: lower p95 -> less batching -> more capacity -> higher cost.
[04:01] Alex Chen: Exactly. That's where our Optimize recommendations come in: choose quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit), kernel selection, and KV caching to reduce per-token work. Also fallback to a smaller model for non-critical calls to save headroom.
[04:14] Dana Park: We're worried about cold-starts during a sudden spike. Do you support pre-warming or burst capacity?
[04:19] Sofia Patel: Yes. Dedicated offers burst capacity and configurable autoscaling policies. You can set reserved baseline for steady-state and permit burst nodes for short spikes, with optional overprovisioning. We also support canary model rollouts and automatic fallback if capacity is constrained.
[04:33] Maya Singh: For our campaign peaks (1,100 concurrent), what sizing ballpark would you give?
[04:38] Jon Ruiz: Based on your tokens profile (280 in, 150 out), assuming we aim for 200ms p95 server-side and moderate KV reuse, rough starting point is 8–12 GPUs of current gen or equivalent Dedicated vCPUs/GPUs, with burst capacity up to another 6–8 GPUs. This is very approximate; the benchmark will refine it.
[04:58] Liam O'Neill: Could we try a hybrid approach: Dedicated for primary traffic, Hosted for opportunistic burst overflow?
[05:03] Alex Chen: You can do policy-based routing — route critical traffic to Dedicated and overflow to Hosted or Private depending on latency tolerance and data residency. There's also automated fallback to smaller model variants.
[05:13] Maya Singh: Network hops matter for us. We have users in EU and NA — would multi-region deployment be required to hit p95?
[05:20] Sofia Patel: For tight p95 targets we recommend regional endpoints close to users. Redwood supports multi-region routing and cross-region failover. For EU-resident data, keep inference within EU region in Private or Dedicated EU pools.
[05:34] Omar Rahman: Any gotchas on encryption in transit? We need TLS mutual auth for internal traffic.
[05:39] Jon Ruiz: Mutual TLS can be configured in Private deployments and in Dedicated with customer-managed endpoints. Hosted supports TLS with mTLS for enterprise plans. We'll include the cert rotation flow in the docs.
[05:50] Dana Park: About benchmarks: how granular are the p95 metrics? We need per-route p95 and token-level breakdowns.
[05:57] Sofia Patel: We export per-route/model p95, latency histograms, token emission times, and request traces. You can also pull token-level cost breakdowns.
[06:07] Liam O'Neill: Do you support streaming codecs / chunk sizes? Our frontend expects 40–60ms chunk cadence.
[06:13] Jon Ruiz: We surface streaming chunking controls; client-side aggregation affects perceived latency. If you want 40–60ms cadence we need to make sure server-side per-token emission is under that cadence and network layers add minimal jitter. We'll test this in the replay.
[06:27] Alex Chen: Are there budget constraints or preferred procurement path?
[06:30] Maya Singh: We'll likely go through a procurement review, procurement needs an initial estimate for committed capacity. We prefer a 12-month committed Dedicated contract if the numbers make sense.
[06:40] Alex Chen: Ok, we'll model committed vs burst pricing in the proposal.
[06:43] Dana Park: Any concerns about model drift or quality regressions with quantization? We can't accept degraded output quality for core flows.
[06:50] Sofia Patel: We do quality regressions monitoring tied to prompt sets. For critical flows we usually keep full-precision models or validated quantized profiles. Optimize can suggest quantization but only after you validate on a held-out eval set.
[07:03] Maya Singh: Good. For the benchmark we will provide 2 hours of representative traffic first and then the 48-hour replay.
[07:10] Liam O'Neill: On telemetry side, can we hook up our tracing? We use Datadog + Jaeger.
[07:15] Jon Ruiz: Yes, we expose tracing hooks and logs; we can send spans to your tracing backend or you can ingest Redwood traces via OTLP.
[07:22] Omar Rahman: Last security question: are requests de-identified in Hosted? We want to avoid PII leaving our environment.
[07:29] Sofia Patel: Hosted can be configured to avoid storing raw payloads and apply tokenization/anonymization at the edge. For full control, Private keeps data entirely in your VPC. We'll note that in the security pack.
[07:40] Alex Chen: Ok, let's capture the clear next steps. We'll send pricing and a benchmark plan. Sofia, you'll draft the benchmark and Jon will handle the replay ingestion steps.
[07:50] Sofia Patel: Yep. Plan will include success criteria: server-side p95 <= 200ms for streaming on critical routes, token loss < 0.1% and sustained tokens/sec target > X (we'll compute after we see the dataset).
[08:04] Maya Singh: One more nuance — some flows are multi-turn with long KV state; how does Redwood handle KV cache eviction?
[08:11] Jon Ruiz: We allow configurable KV cache TTLs and shard-aware eviction policies; on Dedicated you can tune memory to keep larger KV caches. That helps reduce recomputation.
[08:22] Liam O'Neill: What's the lead time for Dedicated capacity?
[08:25] Alex Chen: For reserved Dedicated pools it's typically 2–4 weeks depending on region and hardware spec; for urgent proofs we can spin up a pilot cluster faster via Hosted or temporary Dedicated rentals.
[08:37] Dana Park: Great. Any compliance docs we should expect?
[08:40] Sofia Patel: We'll share SOC2 attestation, EU data flow notes, KMS/HSM integration guides, and audit log sample.
[08:50] Maya Singh: Sounds good.
[08:52] Alex Chen: Thanks all. Quick recap of agreed items: Verdance to share anonymized replay + representative 2-hour sample; Redwood to send Dedicated pricing, benchmark plan, and SOC2/KMS docs. We'll schedule the benchmark kickoff for next week.
[09:06] Dana Park: OK we'll aim to have the sample by Thursday.
[09:09] Alex Chen: Perfect. Any final questions?
[09:12] Omar Rahman: Not for now. We'll review the security pack.
[09:15] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with next steps.

Summary of technical notes (raw):
- Customer target: server-side p95 ~200ms for streaming token emission; client-perceived p95 ~250ms
- Steady-state concurrency: ~120; peak concurrency: ~1,100
- Typical tokens: prompt 280, response 150
- Suggested starter sizing: 8–12 current gen GPUs for baseline, +6–8 GPU burst for peaks (subject to benchmark)
- Tradeoffs: lower p95 reduces usable batching and reduces tokens/sec per GPU -> require more capacity -> higher cost
- Recommendations: Dedicated for primary traffic with burst autoscale and Hosted fallback; regionally colocated Dedicated for EU customers; KV prefix caching to cut per-token compute; validated quantization for non-critical flows

Action items (as above):
- Alex Chen: send pricing and burst options (due 2026-07-07)
- Sofia Patel: benchmark plan + success criteria (due 2026-07-08)
- Jon Ruiz: ingestion steps for traffic replay and OTLP tracing hooks (due 2026-07-08)
- Maya Singh: provide anonymized traffic sample and 48-hour replay permission (due 2026-07-08)
- Omar Rahman: confirm compliance/residency specifics (due 2026-07-10)

Questions noted during call:
- Can Redwood guarantee p95 with burst scenarios? (Answer: SLA-backed targets on Dedicated; system offers burst policies but need tests)
- Cold-start mitigation strategies? (Pre-warm, overprovision, burst nodes)
- Quantization impact on quality? (Validated via eval sets; monitor regressions)

Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts present (names and acronyms sometimes garbled, e.g., KV cache -> K V cache, HSM -> H S M). Some timestamps approximate.
